hypothesis: The eyewitness 'unbiased instruction' repair does not transfer to LLM pooled verifiers: a wording-only caution ('the correct answer may or may not be among these candidates') cuts the target-absent choosing rate by less than 10 percentage points, while stating a numeric base rate ('about half of the pools in this study contain no correct answer') cuts it by at least 20 points. So the judge's choosing is set by its implied prior that a correct candidate is present, not by permission to reject.
gap_with_citations: Source science (verified this session): Malpass and Devine (1981) is the standard citation for 'may or may not be present' instructions. Steblay (1997, Law and Human Behavior 21(3):283-297), a meta-analysis of 22 tests and 2,588 witnesses, found that cautionary instructions reduce target-absent errors (about 25 percent fewer by a Steblay summary) with a near-zero average effect on target-present hits. Clark (2005) disputes the target-present result. LLM side (from corpus): the corpus lineup runs (corpus/02 paper.md; corpus/08 FINDING.md) gave judges an explicit NONE option and still saw 70 percent (arithmetic) and 29 percent (hypotheses) target-absent choosing, but never manipulated the instruction. Adjacent MCQA work (verified this session, abstract level): Goral and Wisnios (arXiv 2409.00113) used a 'answer may not be among the options' prompt and still found a large gap. Tam et al., 'None of the Above, Less of the Right' (Findings ACL 2025), report a 30 to 50 percent drop when NA is correct. Neither work separates a wording caution from a numeric base rate, and neither studies accept/reject verifier pools.
prediction: Haiku pooled judge, target-absent pools of 4: choosing rate in the baseline arm is about 0.5 or more. The CAUTION arm is within 10 pp of baseline. The BASE-RATE arm is at least 20 pp below baseline. Target-present hit rate in the BASE-RATE arm drops by no more than 8 pp, so the base-rate repair is a criterion shift that buys a better hit/false-ID tradeoff than the caution does.
kill_criterion: Kill if baseline minus CAUTION is 10 pp or more (point estimate, with a 95 percent paired-bootstrap CI excluding 5 pp), OR if baseline minus BASE-RATE is under 20 pp. Either outcome falsifies the claim that the two instructions differ.
smallest_experiment: Items: 160 CRUXEval output prediction (github.com/facebookresearch/cruxeval, reachable by git this session; 800 Python functions, gold by executing the function on CPU) items where haiku solver sampling (5 samples per item at temperature defaults, about 800 haiku calls) yields at least 3 distinct wrong outputs. Pools: a target-absent pool of 4 wrongs and a target-present pool of gold plus 3 wrongs. Arms: BASELINE (corpus prompt with NONE option), CAUTION, BASE-RATE, crossed with TA/TP: 160 x 3 x 2 = 960 haiku judge calls. Sonnet replication on 60 TA items x 3 arms = 180 calls. Primary test: paired within-pool McNemar plus a cluster bootstrap over items.
why_it_matters: Every co-scientist ranking prompt already says something like 'none may be good', and the corpus shows it does not work. If a numeric prior works where a caution does not, the cheapest fix for discovery-regime false picks is to tell the ranker the realistic hit rate of its generator.
scoop_risk: Medium. MCQA 'none of the above' work is close, but it does not compare caution against a stated base rate and does not use verifier pools.

hypothesis: A 'blank lineup' negative control (Wells 1984) screens LLM verification at the item level. Show the judge, in a separate fresh call, a pool of 4 machine-certified wrong candidates for the same item. Whether it picks from that blank pool predicts whether it falsely picks from the real target-absent pool, so a cheap negative control flags items where pooled verification cannot be trusted.
gap_with_citations: Source science (verified this session): Wells (1984), 'The Psychology of Lineup Identifications', J. Applied Social Psychology 14(2):89-103, doi 10.1111/j.1559-1816.1984.tb02223.x. In 192 students, witnesses who picked from a blank (all-innocent) lineup were less credible on the subsequent real lineup, and witnesses who rejected it made fewer false identifications. Palmer et al. later studied 'the information gained from witnesses' responses to an initial blank lineup'. LLM side (from corpus): corpus/08 and corpus/02 measured target-absent choosing but no per-item negative control. The atlas gap list (corpus/11 out_C C-G10: what makes a wrong hypothesis an attractor is unmeasured) leaves item-level predictors of false picks open. No LLM paper using a blank-lineup control turned up in this session's searches (absence not proven).
prediction: Fresh-call design. Per item, one haiku judge sees the BLANK pool (4 wrong outputs produced by running mutated versions of the function, each certified different from gold) and a separate haiku judge sees the REAL target-absent pool (4 real solver wrong outputs), each with 3 replicate calls. P(real-pool false pick | majority picked from blank) minus P(real-pool false pick | majority rejected blank) is at least +0.20. Blank rejection does not lower target-present hits by more than 5 pp, compared with blank pickers' hits.
kill_criterion: Kill if the item-level difference is under +0.10, or if its 95 percent bootstrap CI over items includes 0. Also kill if blank-pool choosing is above 0.9 or below 0.1, since a split that degenerate makes the screen uninformative.
smallest_experiment: 200 CRUXEval output prediction (github.com/facebookresearch/cruxeval, reachable by git this session; 800 Python functions, gold by executing the function on CPU) items. Mutants: 3 to 6 operator and constant mutations per function, executed on CPU, keeping outputs that differ from gold and from each other. Calls: BLANK 200 x 3 + REAL-TA 200 x 3 + REAL-TP 200 x 3 = 1,800 haiku calls, plus a sonnet judge on 100 items x 3 conditions = 300 calls. Analysis: logistic regression of real false pick on blank pick, with item-difficulty covariate (isolated accept rate from 200 x 4 isolated calls, which can be subsampled).
why_it_matters: Gives automated research pipelines a deployable, ground-truth-free reliability check: plant a known-null pool next to the real one. It turns the lineup finding from a warning into an instrument.
scoop_risk: Low to medium. Decoy and knockoff ideas exist in statistics (corpus/11 D-D2 proposes knockoffs for analyst agents), but nobody has used per-item blank lineups to screen an LLM verifier.

hypothesis: When an LLM verifier judges a stream of items in one context, the prevalence of wrong items shifts its criterion, and the direction follows prevalence-induced concept change (Levari et al. 2018) rather than the low-prevalence miss effect from visual search (Wolfe et al. 2005). When errors are rare in the batch, the judge widens its concept of 'error' and falsely rejects more correct items. It does not miss more of the rare errors.
gap_with_citations: Source science (verified this session): Levari, Gilbert, Wilson, Sievers, Amodio and Wheatley (2018), Science 360:1465-1467, doi 10.1126/science.aap8731. As blue dots, threatening faces or unethical requests became rare, people expanded the category, and the effect persisted despite warnings and incentives. Wolfe, Horowitz and Kenner (2005), Nature 435:439-440, doi 10.1038/435439a, report target miss rates of 11 percent (common), 25 percent (rare) and 52 percent (very rare) in baggage-like search. The visual-search literature reads this as a criterion shift and lower quitting thresholds. LLM side: this session's search found no study that varies batch error prevalence for an LLM judge. The related work found was arXiv 2512.08121 (prevalence and judge metrics, from search snippets) and anchoring and history effects (arXiv 2608.25869 and 2605.22714, from search snippets only; the abstracts could not be fetched because arxiv.org is blocked). The two human literatures predict opposite signs of the criterion shift, which makes this a discriminating test.
prediction: Batches of 20 (function, input, claimed output) items in one prompt, each judged CORRECT or WRONG, with 4 embedded probe items whose identity is held fixed across conditions. Error prevalence among the 16 fillers is 10, 50 or 90 percent. In the 10 percent condition, the false-WRONG rate on correct probes is at least 1.5 times the 50 percent condition's rate, and the SDT criterion c on probes shifts toward 'wrong' by at least 0.2. Probe d-prime changes by less than 0.25.
kill_criterion: Kill if the criterion shift between the 10 and 50 percent conditions is under 0.1 in absolute value (95 percent bootstrap CI over probe items includes 0), OR if it goes in the Wolfe direction (more misses of wrong probes at low prevalence, with c shifting toward 'correct' by 0.1 or more). The second outcome supports the rival transfer.
smallest_experiment: Probe set: 80 CRUXEval output prediction (github.com/facebookresearch/cruxeval, reachable by git this session; 800 Python functions, gold by executing the function on CPU) items, 40 with gold output and 40 with a real haiku-solver wrong output, chosen where isolated haiku accuracy is between 0.35 and 0.85 (selected with 80 x 5 = 400 isolated haiku calls). Fillers: 400 other items with known correct or wrong outputs. Conditions: 3 prevalences x 160 batches (each probe appears in 8 batches per condition) = 480 haiku calls. Sonnet replication: 3 x 50 = 150 calls. Analysis: mixed-effects probit with probe random effects.
why_it_matters: Verifiers in agent loops see streams whose error rate falls as the system improves. If the concept of 'error' expands as errors become rare, judged quality plateaus by construction, and the judge's rejection rate stays flat even as true quality rises. This is a measurement artefact in self-improvement loops.
scoop_risk: Low. No LLM prevalence-manipulation study turned up in this session's searches. History and anchoring papers are adjacent but do not manipulate base rate or separate c from d-prime.

hypothesis: LLM code reviewers show 'subsequent search misses' (satisfaction of search) from radiology. A subtle bug is detected less often when the same function also contains a salient bug than when the subtle bug is the only defect, and the miss is larger when the two bugs are of different kinds (Berbaum's perceptual-set account).
gap_with_citations: Source science (verified this session): Adamo, Gereke, Shomstein and Schmidt (2021), Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications, a review titled 'From satisfaction of search to subsequent search misses' (PMC8403090). It credits Adamo, Cain and Mitroff (2013) with the term SSM. It says Berbaum et al. (1990, 1991) found radiologists search for targets similar to the first one found, so dissimilar second targets are missed more. It reports that satisfaction, perceptual-set and resource-depletion accounts each have partial support. LLM side: this session's search found no controlled single-versus-dual-bug detection study for LLM reviewers, only practitioner anecdotes and a non-peer-reviewed Zenodo preprint on low single-model recall. arXiv 2606.26529 ('inattentional gap in task conditioned AI models') turned up in search but was not read, and could be adjacent.
prediction: Haiku reviewer asked to list every bug with line numbers. P(detect subtle bug B | B alone) minus P(detect B | salient bug A plus B) is at least +0.10. The deficit is at least 0.05 larger when A and B differ in kind (for example, A is a wrong operator and B is a boundary-condition error) than when they are the same kind. Sonnet shows a deficit at least half the size of haiku's (the effect does not vanish with scale).
kill_criterion: Kill if the haiku B-detection deficit is under +0.05, or its 95 percent cluster-bootstrap CI over functions includes 0. The dissimilarity sub-claim is killed separately if the interaction is under 0.02.
smallest_experiment: 120 functions from HumanEval (github.com/openai/human-eval, reachable by git this session) with their unit tests. For each, inject a salient bug A and a subtle bug B, and verify on CPU that each alone fails at least one test and that A plus B fails. Half the pairs are same-kind and half different-kind. Conditions: A-only, B-only, A+B, 120 x 3 conditions x 3 reps = 1,080 haiku calls. Sonnet: 80 x 3 conditions = 240 calls. Detection is scored programmatically: a reported line range covering the bug's line.
why_it_matters: Multi-agent review pipelines often stop after a reviewer finds 'the' bug, and verify-then-revise loops fix one defect per round. If finding one bug suppresses finding the next, single-pass reviewer recall is systematically overstated on multi-defect code, and the radiology countermeasures (a checklist second pass, or masking the found region) become testable interventions.
scoop_risk: Low to medium. There is anecdotal practitioner discussion. No controlled LLM SSM measurement surfaced.

hypothesis: Serial verification in one prompt, the mitigation the corpus recommends, has autocorrelated verdicts. The direction separates two human transfers: assimilation (serial dependence in perception, Fischer and Whitney 2014) or alternation (the gambler's fallacy in asylum judges, loan officers and umpires, Chen, Moskowitz and Shue 2016). We predict positive dependence: the judge is more likely to ACCEPT an item when its previous verdict was ACCEPT, holding item identity fixed.
gap_with_citations: Source science (verified this session): Chen, Moskowitz and Shue (2016), QJE 131(3):1181-1241, found negative autocorrelation in decisions that is unrelated to case merit, and stronger after streaks and when consecutive cases look alike. Fischer and Whitney (2014), Nature Neuroscience 17(5), doi 10.1038/nn.3689, found perception pulled toward recent input. From corpus: corpus/02 paper.md section 4.5 found a serial-in-one-prompt probe cut false accepts to 0.012 and recommends serial verification. Corpus/08 FINDING.md section 3 found it did not help on hypotheses. Neither run tested whether serial verdicts are independent. LLM adjacent (search snippets only): arXiv 2608.25869 (prior scores anchor judges) and arXiv 2605.22714 (accumulated message history biases later judgments). Neither, as far as the snippets show, estimates within-item lag-1 dependence under randomized orders.
prediction: Batches of 12 CRUXEval verification items in random orders, with each item appearing in at least 10 different orders. Within-item lag-1 effect: P(ACCEPT_i | verdict_{i-1}=ACCEPT) minus P(ACCEPT_i | verdict_{i-1}=REJECT) is at least +0.05, estimated with item fixed effects and controlling for the gold status of item i-1. The effect is larger when items i-1 and i come from the same function family (the similarity moderator Chen et al. report).
kill_criterion: Kill the positive-dependence claim if the 95 percent CI upper bound of the within-item lag-1 coefficient is below +0.02. If the estimate is significantly negative (CI upper bound below 0), report it as the gambler's-fallacy transfer instead.
smallest_experiment: 240 CRUXEval output prediction (github.com/facebookresearch/cruxeval, reachable by git this session; 800 Python functions, gold by executing the function on CPU) (input, output) claims, half correct and half real haiku-solver wrongs. 400 haiku batch calls of 12 items each (4,800 verdicts; every item appears in about 20 orders), plus 120 sonnet batch calls. Analysis: conditional logit with item fixed effects, a lag-1 own-verdict regressor and lag-1 gold, with the lagged verdict instrumented by lagged gold as a robustness check against reflection.
why_it_matters: Serial verification is the cheapest lineup mitigation in the corpus. If its verdicts carry streak dependence, then batch order changes outcomes, error rates measured on batched judges are not exchangeable, and ensembles of batched judges are more correlated than they look.
scoop_risk: Medium. History and anchoring effects in LLM judges are being published (2605.22714, 2608.25869), but the within-item randomized-order lag-1 estimate and the assimilation-versus-alternation contrast appear open.

hypothesis: Double-blind administration matters in multi-agent verification. When the orchestrator that formats a candidate pool for the judge knows which candidate is the 'suspect' (the lead agent's preferred answer), and is told not to reveal it, the judge picks that candidate more often than when the orchestrator is blind. The leak is largest in target-absent pools, where the judge is guessing.
gap_with_citations: Source science (verified this session, abstract level): Greathouse and Kovera (2009), Law and Human Behavior 33:70-82. With 234 witness/administrator pairs, single-blind administration raised suspect identifications most under simultaneous lineups with biased instructions. Single-blind administrators showed more biasing behaviors, and the diagnosticity of suspect IDs was about double under double-blind administration. Wixted and Wells (2017, PSPI) list double-blind testing among the 'pristine' conditions. LLM side: preference leakage (Li et al., arXiv 2502.01534, ICLR 2026; verified this session by search snippet) concerns generator-judge relatedness, not an intermediary that knows the favored candidate. No study of orchestrator-knowledge leakage turned up in this session's searches.
prediction: A sonnet administrator rewrites a 4-candidate pool (answer plus a 2-sentence rationale each) into a 'neutral summary for the reviewer'. In the SINGLE-BLIND arm it is told 'candidate X is the lead agent's answer; do not reveal or favor it', with X a random wrong candidate. In DOUBLE-BLIND it gets no designation. In target-absent pools, P(haiku judge picks X) under SINGLE-BLIND minus P(picks the same candidate) under DOUBLE-BLIND is at least +0.08. In target-present pools the difference is at most half as large.
kill_criterion: Kill if the target-absent difference is under +0.03, or its 95 percent paired bootstrap CI over pools includes 0.
smallest_experiment: 150 CRUXEval output prediction (github.com/facebookresearch/cruxeval, reachable by git this session; 800 Python functions, gold by executing the function on CPU) target-absent pools and 75 target-present pools built from real haiku-solver wrong outputs. Administrator calls (sonnet): 225 pools x 2 arms = 450. To fit 'a few hundred', start with 100 TA plus 50 TP, which is 300 sonnet calls. Judge calls (haiku): 300 summaries x 3 reps = 900. Manipulation check: a haiku 'detective' guesses X from each summary alone (300 calls), giving a text-level leak rate. Analysis: paired by pool; designation X is randomized, so the null is exact.
why_it_matters: Co-scientist and orchestrator architectures routinely have the proposing or lead agent prepare the materials the critic sees. If knowledge of the favored candidate leaks even under an explicit no-leak instruction, blinding the formatting agent is a zero-cost architectural fix, and unblinded pipelines overstate how independent their verification is.
scoop_risk: Low. Experimenter-expectancy and blinding in LLM orchestration did not surface. The preference-leakage literature is related but concerns a different channel.

hypothesis: Deliberating LLM verifier panels show the MacCoun and Kerr leniency asymmetry, and it is caused by the stated standard of proof. Under an 'accept only if correct beyond reasonable doubt' rule, evenly split (2:2) haiku panels resolve toward REJECT much more often than toward ACCEPT. Under a 'preponderance' rule the asymmetry shrinks. The standard of proof in the instruction, not the content, therefore decides who wins split deliberations.
gap_with_citations: Source science (verified this session, abstract level): MacCoun and Kerr (1988), 'Asymmetric influence in mock jury deliberation: Jurors' bias for leniency', JPSP 54(1):21-33. Experiment 2 manipulated reasonable-doubt versus preponderance instructions to test whether the standard causes the asymmetry. A later synthesis of 13 studies reported acquittal about 4 times as likely as conviction for juries starting evenly split. Kerr and MacCoun (2012, 'Is the leniency asymmetry really dead?') find a smaller but present effect in real juries. From corpus: corpus/11 out_B B-G8 says group-psychology mechanisms (social decision schemes and others) are cited but not carried over as manipulations, and B-G2 leaves the direction of persuasion asymmetry open. LLM side: LLM jury papers (arXiv 2605.01986 '12 Angry AI Agents', from search snippets) report hung-jury defaults, and none surfaced that manipulates the standard of proof.
prediction: Panels of 4 haiku agents each start with their own real independent first-round verdict and argument on a CRUXEval claim, selected so 2 say ACCEPT and 2 say REJECT. Two deliberation rounds follow, then a final individual vote, with majority as the verdict. Under REASONABLE-DOUBT, P(final REJECT | 2:2 start) is at least 0.65. Under PREPONDERANCE it is at most 0.55. The difference is at least 15 pp and holds separately for correct and wrong claims, so it is not driven by truth.
kill_criterion: Kill if the REASONABLE-DOUBT minus PREPONDERANCE difference in P(final REJECT | 2:2) is under 8 pp, or its 95 percent cluster-bootstrap CI over items includes 0.
smallest_experiment: Seed pool: 140 CRUXEval output prediction (github.com/facebookresearch/cruxeval, reachable by git this session; 800 Python functions, gold by executing the function on CPU) claims (70 correct, 70 real wrong outputs) with haiku isolated accept rates between 0.3 and 0.7. Independent haiku first-round verdicts under each standard: 140 x 8 x 2 = 2,240 calls, keeping items with at least 2 accepts and 2 rejects. Deliberation: about 100 items x 2 standards x 2 panel reps x 4 agents x 2 rounds = 3,200 haiku calls. Sonnet panel check: 30 items x 2 standards x 4 agents x 2 rounds = 480 calls, cut to 15 items (240) if budget binds.
why_it_matters: Debate and panel verification are oversight's main multi-agent primitives. If an instruction's burden-of-proof wording mechanically decides split panels, then panel accuracy gains reported in the literature confound deliberation with a criterion shift. Designers could also choose the standard of proof to match the cost of false accepts versus false rejects.
scoop_risk: Low to medium. LLM jury simulations exist, but no standard-of-proof manipulation of split-panel resolution surfaced.

hypothesis: Spectrum bias (Ransohoff and Feinstein 1978) distorts LLM verifier evaluation. Specificity measured on easy-spectrum negatives (random or mutation-generated wrong outputs) overstates specificity on hard-spectrum negatives (real wrong outputs from the generator being verified) by at least 20 pp. The ranking of verifier configurations (haiku, sonnet, opus x isolated or pooled) changes between spectra.
gap_with_citations: Source science (verified this session): Ransohoff and Feinstein (1978), NEJM 299(17):926-930, doi 10.1056/NEJM197810262991705. Narrow diseased and non-diseased spectra inflate sensitivity and specificity. A 2016 BMJ review (PMC4916916) prefers 'spectrum effect'. LLM side (this session, search snippets): arXiv 2512.02389 reports synthetic error injection behaves differently from on-policy errors for self-correction. arXiv 2604.01993 (SAFE) reports that verifiers trained on injected errors generalize worse. Neither measures how evaluation-set spectrum changes judge rankings. From corpus: corpus/02 paper.md section 3 used 8.6 percent digit-perturbation synthetics and reported a sensitivity analysis, but no spectrum contrast. Corpus/11 out_C C-G12 notes hypothesis benchmarks rarely certify that their negatives are false.
prediction: On 150 CRUXEval items, each verifier configuration's specificity on EASY negatives (outputs of mutated functions, certified different from gold) exceeds its specificity on HARD negatives (the modal wrong output of 5 haiku solver samples) by at least 20 pp for haiku and at least 10 pp for opus. Kendall tau between the 6 configurations' balanced-accuracy rankings on EASY and HARD is below 0.6.
kill_criterion: Kill if the haiku specificity gap is under 10 pp (95 percent CI includes 10), or if tau is 0.8 or higher with the opus gap under 5 pp. Together those mean spectrum does not change conclusions.
smallest_experiment: 150 CRUXEval output prediction (github.com/facebookresearch/cruxeval, reachable by git this session; 800 Python functions, gold by executing the function on CPU) items; haiku solver 5 samples each (750 calls); keep items with a real wrong. Isolated verification: gold, easy-negative, hard-negative per item. Haiku 150 x 3 x 2 reps = 900; sonnet 100 x 3 = 300; opus 60 x 3 = 180. Pooled verification (gold + easy + hard + one more hard, pool of 4) for haiku 150 x 2 = 300 and sonnet 60 = 60. Analysis: paired bootstrap over items, plus Kendall tau with bootstrap CI.
why_it_matters: Verifier choice in MAS (which model, which protocol) is made from benchmark specificity. If benchmark negatives are easier than the system's own mistakes, every selection-law calculation that plugs in benchmark f underestimates false accepts, and model-selection decisions may invert.
scoop_risk: Medium. The 'synthetic negatives are easier' intuition is widespread and partly shown for training. A clean evaluation-side spectrum contrast with ranking inversion across Claude tiers did not surface.

hypothesis: The eyewitness confidence-accuracy result (high-confidence initial IDs are accurate under pristine conditions, Wixted and Wells 2017) does not transfer to pooled LLM verification. Pooling inflates false picks at the top confidence level, not only at low confidence. Restricting to maximum-confidence picks does not bring the target-absent false-pick rate back to the isolated rate, but serial presentation does.
gap_with_citations: Source science (verified this session): Wixted and Wells (2017), PSPI, 'The Relationship Between Eyewitness Confidence and Identification Accuracy: A New Synthesis'. Under pristine procedures (fair lineup, double-blind, 'may not be present' caution, immediate confidence), high-confidence suspect IDs are highly accurate. Under non-pristine conditions, even high-confidence IDs are compromised. Confidence-accuracy characteristic (CAC) analysis is attributed to Mickes (2015, via citing papers; the original was not retrieved). From corpus: corpus/11 out_X X-G15 says eyewitness confidence science stops at the lineup and initial-confidence diagnosticity is not carried over, and X-D5 proposes post-agreement feedback. Corpus/02 measured pooled versus isolated f without confidence. This hypothesis is the CAC piece of X-G15 applied to the pooled-versus-serial manipulation.
prediction: Haiku judges give a 0 to 100 confidence with each PICK. In target-absent pools of 4, the rate of picks at confidence 90 or above is at least 3 times the isolated rate of accepts at 90 or above on the same wrong candidates. In the serial-in-one-prompt arm, the high-confidence false-accept rate is within 1.5 times the isolated rate. The CAC curve (accuracy of picks by confidence bin, target-present plus target-absent) for pooled judges stays below 0.8 accuracy in the top bin.
kill_criterion: Kill if the pooled-to-isolated ratio of confidence-90-plus false accepts is under 1.5, or if top-bin pooled CAC accuracy is 0.9 or higher (which would mean high confidence remains diagnostic and confidence gating is a sufficient fix).
smallest_experiment: 160 CRUXEval output prediction (github.com/facebookresearch/cruxeval, reachable by git this session; 800 Python functions, gold by executing the function on CPU) items with at least 3 real wrong outputs. Arms: ISOLATED (each candidate alone; 160 x 4 = 640), POOL-TA (160), POOL-TP (160), SERIAL-TA (160), each with 2 reps = 2,240 haiku calls. Sonnet on POOL-TA, POOL-TP and ISOLATED for 60 items (60 x 6 = 360 calls). Analysis: within-candidate ratios with item-cluster bootstrap, and CAC curves with Wilson CIs.
why_it_matters: Pipelines commonly gate on judge confidence ('only accept picks with confidence 90 or above'). If pooling creates confident false picks, confidence gating does not repair the lineup problem, and only presentation format does.
scoop_risk: Medium. LLM verbalized-confidence calibration is heavily studied, but pooled versus isolated versus serial CAC on target-absent pools did not surface. Corpus/11 already lists X-G15, so internal overlap is high.
